notes.html:
🧭 Scope. 07-http-semantics/68-timeouts-retries-backoff.md owns the backoff and jitter mathematics — the four jitter strategies and their variance properties. This note owns when a retry is legal, how many you may afford, and what happens across a fleet — the gating, the budget and the amplification. Cross-referenced rather than repeated.

📚 Reference Links

  • Retry budgets and the amplification argument — Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

  • Client-side throttling, the fleet-level control — Google SRE Book: Handling Overload

  • Why retries turn a brownout into an outage — Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

  • What makes a retry legal — RFC 9110 §9.2.2: Idempotent Methods

  • Bonus — AWS Well-Architected: REL05-BP03 Control and limit retry calls

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which failures are always safe to retry? Connection-level ones — the request never reached the application, so nothing happened.
Which method property permits a retry? Idempotent (RFC 9110 §9.2.2). A POST needs an idempotency key to qualify (Item 155).
What is a retry budget? A cap on retries as a fraction of successful requests — typically ~10%, fleet-wide.
Amplification across 3 hops at 3 attempts each? 3³ = 27 requests reach the deepest service for one user request.
Why is a timeout the most dangerous thing to retry? You cannot tell whether the work completed. Retrying may duplicate an effect.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three questions gate every retry. Is it legal? — connection failures always are, because the request never arrived; responses are retryable only if the operation is idempotent. Can you afford it? — a retry budget caps retries as a fraction of successes, around ten percent, so a struggling dependency does not receive multiplied load. What does it do at fleet scale? — attempts multiply along a call chain, so three hops retrying three times each sends twenty-seven requests to the deepest service. The backoff and jitter mathematics live in the Section 7 note; the gating, budget and amplification live here.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Which failures may you retry, and why is a timeout the hard case?

🎯 Really testing: whether you reason about what the server may already have done, rather than about error codes.

Sort by what the server could have done. A connection-level failure — refused, reset before the request was sent, DNS failure — means the request never reached the application, so nothing happened and retrying is unconditionally safe regardless of the operation. A 429 or 503 with Retry-After is an explicit invitation: the server is telling you it did not process the request and when to come back.

A timeout is the hard case because it tells you nothing about the server's state. The request may never have arrived, may have arrived and be executing, or may have completed with the response lost on the way back. Retrying a timed-out GET is fine because repeating it changes nothing. Retrying a timed-out POST /payments may charge a customer twice, and the client cannot distinguish that case from the safe one. This is precisely where idempotency keys earn their place: they convert the unanswerable question into a safe one by making the server able to recognise a repeat (Item 155).

A 500 is ambiguous in the same way but usually worse: the operation may have partially completed. And a 400 or 404 must never be retried at all — the request is wrong, and repeating it wastes capacity while guaranteeing the same answer. That last case sounds obvious and is a common defect in generic retry wrappers that retry on "any error".

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How many retries, and where in the chain?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up after any retry-storm postmortem.

🎯 Really testing: whether you think about the whole chain rather than about one client's configuration.

The count is bounded by the timeout budget before it is bounded by anything else: attempts × (timeout + backoff) < caller's remaining budget (Item 149). At a 600ms timeout inside a 1500ms budget, two attempts fit and three do not. So "three retries" is not a default you can adopt — it is a number the budget either affords or does not.

The placement question matters more and gets less attention. Retrying at every hop multiplies. Three hops at three attempts each is 3³ = 27 requests to the deepest service for one user request, and that multiplication arrives exactly when the deepest service is already struggling. The discipline is to retry at one layer, usually the outermost one that still knows enough to decide safety, and to have inner layers fail fast and propagate. Where a mesh or gateway also retries, that is a layer — configure it or the client, not both (Section 13, Item 141).

The fleet-level control is a retry budget rather than a per-request count: cap retries at roughly 10% of successful requests, measured over a window, and stop retrying when the ratio is exceeded. Google's client-side throttling is the canonical form. Its virtue is that it is self-limiting under exactly the conditions where per-request counts do the most harm — when everything is failing, a per-request policy triples the load, while a budget lets it decay toward zero.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

A dependency degrades to a 40% error rate. Trace what retries do to it.

📍 Seen in the wild: the retry-storm postmortem, and the clearest argument for budgets.

Without a budget, retries convert a partial degradation into a total outage. At a 40% error rate with three attempts, the expected requests per user request is 1 + 0.4 + 0.16 = 1.56 — a 56% load increase arriving at a service that is already failing 40% of what it receives. That extra load raises latency, which raises the error rate, which raises the retry rate, which raises the load. The loop has positive feedback and it converges on 100% failure with the service receiving roughly three times its normal traffic.

It presents as a service that gets worse after the initial trigger has passed. The signature is a request-rate graph that rises while the success-rate graph falls — an inverse correlation that is unmistakable once you look for it, and impossible to explain by demand, because users did not suddenly send more traffic. Utilisation is at 100%, goodput is near zero, and restarting the service produces a brief recovery followed by immediate re-collapse as the accumulated client retries arrive at once.

The remedies in order of leverage: a retry budget so the retry rate decays as the success rate falls; jitter so the retries that do happen are not synchronised into waves (the mathematics are in Section 7, Item 68); circuit breaking so clients stop calling a failing dependency at all (Item 151); and load shedding at the server so it protects a serving fraction rather than failing everything equally. The budget is the one that directly breaks the feedback loop, which is why it belongs in the client library rather than in each service's configuration.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the retry policy for a path that calls a model provider and a payments service.

🎯 Really testing: whether you apply different policies to different call semantics rather than one global wrapper.

The dominating constraint is that these two calls have opposite retry profiles and a single policy will be wrong for one of them. The model call is expensive (20-second p99), non-idempotent in effect (a regenerated response costs real money and may differ), and its failures are frequently rate limits. The payments call is fast, strictly non-idempotent, and its failure modes are exactly the ones where a duplicate is unacceptable.

So: for the model call, at most one retry, and only on connection-level failures or an explicit 429/503 with Retry-After — never on a timeout, because at 20 seconds a timeout most likely means the generation is still running and a retry doubles the cost while the first may still land. The budget arithmetic forbids more anyway: two attempts is 40 seconds plus backoff, which exceeds any user-facing budget. For payments, retries are permitted only with an idempotency key, which converts the ambiguous timeout into a safe repeat because the server recognises the key and returns the original result rather than charging again (Item 155).

Across both, a shared retry budget at ~10% of successes with client-side throttling, and retries at one layer only — the service's own client, with the mesh's route-level retries explicitly disabled so the two do not multiply.

The failure I would monitor first is retry rate as a fraction of successes, per dependency, because it is the leading indicator of a storm and the direct measurement of whether the budget is holding. Second is duplicate-effect rate on the payments path — idempotency-key collisions that returned a cached result — because a rising number there means retries are firing on ambiguous outcomes and the key is doing load-bearing work. Third is the inverse correlation between request rate and success rate, which is the storm signature itself.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Failure Did the server act? Retry? Condition
Connection refused / reset before send No Always Unconditionally safe — nothing reached the application
DNS failure No Always Same reasoning
429 / 503 with Retry-After No Yes Honour the header; do not retry sooner
503 without Retry-After Probably not Yes, budgeted Backoff with jitter
Timeout Unknown Only if idempotent, or with an idempotency key The hard case — see Item 155
500 Possibly partially Only if idempotent Ambiguous, and may have left partial state
502 / 504 Unknown Only if idempotent The proxy could not tell either
400 / 404 / 422 Yes, and rejected it Never The request is wrong; repeating wastes capacity
401 / 403 Yes Never (retry after re-auth is a different call) Fix the credential, do not repeat

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Backoff and jitter mathematics are in 07-http-semantics/68-timeouts-retries-backoff.md; the arithmetic below is the amplification and budget half this note owns.

Amplification along a chain is multiplicative. With n hops each permitting k attempts, the deepest service receives up to kⁿ requests per user request: 3 hops × 3 attempts = 27. This is the number to quote, because it makes the case for retrying at one layer more forcefully than any argument about tidiness.

Expected load under a degradation is a geometric series. With failure probability p and up to k attempts, expected requests per user request is 1 + p + p² + … + p^(k−1). At p = 0.4, k = 3 that is 1.56 — a 56% load increase. At p = 0.9 it approaches 2.71, so a service failing almost everything receives nearly triple its normal traffic. Load rises fastest exactly when the service is least able to serve it, which is the positive feedback that makes storms self-sustaining.

A retry budget breaks the feedback because it is denominated in successes. Capping retries at ~10% of successful requests means the retry allowance shrinks as success falls: at 40% success the budget permits far fewer retries than at 99%, and at near-zero success it permits almost none. A per-request attempt count has the opposite property — it multiplies load precisely when everything is failing. That inversion is the whole argument for budgets over counts.

Connection-level retries sit outside all of this. Because the request provably never reached the application, they cannot duplicate an effect and they do not need idempotency reasoning. They should still be budgeted, but their gating question is already answered — which is why the pooling note recommends exactly one of them unconditionally (Item 148).

7. Why It Matters in Production

Retries are the mechanism by which a client either absorbs a transient failure or amplifies a partial one into a total outage. The same code does both; which one you get depends entirely on gating and budget.

The observable that matters is retry rate as a fraction of successful requests, per dependency. It is the direct measurement of the budget, it is the leading indicator of a storm, and almost no client library exports it by default. Its absence is why retry storms are usually diagnosed from the server's request-rate graph rather than from the clients causing them.

The second is the inverse correlation between request rate and success rate. Demand does not rise when a service starts failing — so a request-rate graph climbing while success falls is retries, not users, and recognising that shape shortens a storm postmortem from hours to minutes.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Gating first, budget second, backoff third. The gating is what most wrappers get wrong.
RETRYABLE_STATUS = {429, 503}           # explicit "I did not process this"
NEVER_RETRY      = {400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422}

def should_retry(exc, response, method, has_idempotency_key, budget):
    if not budget.allow():                     # fleet-level: ~10% of successes
        return False
    if exc is not None and exc.reached_application is False:
        return True                            # connection-level: ALWAYS safe
    if response is None:                       # timeout - the ambiguous case
        return method in IDEMPOTENT or has_idempotency_key
    if response.status in NEVER_RETRY:
        return False                           # repeating a rejected request is pure waste
    if response.status in RETRYABLE_STATUS:
        return True
    if 500 <= response.status < 600:
        return method in IDEMPOTENT or has_idempotency_key
    return False

# If the mesh retries too, you have TWO layers multiplying. Pick one.
retryPolicy:
  attempts: 1                      # disabled here - the client owns retries
  retryOn: connect-failure,refused-stream   # connection-level only, never 5xx

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

A three-hop chain at 50 rps when the deepest service degrades to a 40% error rate.

🎬 BROKEN: every hop retries 3x, no budget
📥 [1] 50 rps of user requests
    ▼
📈 [2] hop A: 3 attempts → up to 150 rps toward B
    ▼
📈 [3] hop B: 3 attempts each → up to 450 rps toward C
    │   amplification 3^3 = 27x worst case; expected 1.56^3 ≈ 3.8x at p=0.4
    ▼
💥 [4] C receives ~190 rps against a normal 50. Latency rises, p→0.7
    │   expected multiplier rises to 2.1^3 ≈ 9x. Feedback loop engaged.
    ▼
📉 [5] observed: request rate UP 4x, success rate DOWN to 8%
    │   ← inverse correlation = retries, not demand. Users sent nothing extra.
    ▼
🔁 [6] restart C → 20s of recovery → accumulated client retries arrive → re-collapse

🎬 FIXED: retries at ONE layer, budget at 10% of successes
📥 [7] 50 rps; only hop A retries; B and C fail fast and propagate
    ▼
🛡️ [8] budget: successes fall to 30 rps → retry allowance = 3 rps, not 150
    │   the allowance SHRINKS as success falls — the loop cannot close
    ▼
✅ [9] C receives ~53 rps. Still degraded at p=0.4, but not amplified.
    │   30% of user requests fail. Not 92%.
    ▼
🔍 [10] circuit breaker opens at sustained failure → C's load drops to probes
        → C recovers → breaker half-opens → traffic returns gradually

  1. Step 3 is the number worth memorising. 3³ = 27 is the worst case and ~3.8× the expected case at a 40% error rate, and both arrive at the service least able to absorb them.

  2. Step 5's inverse correlation is the diagnostic. Rising requests with falling success cannot be demand — users did not coordinate a surge at the moment a service degraded. That shape means retries, every time.

  3. Step 6 is why storms outlive their trigger. Clients accumulate pending retries during the outage and release them on recovery, so the first moments after a restart carry more load than steady state — which re-breaks the service and looks like the fix failing.

  4. Step 8 is the budget doing the thing a count cannot. Denominating in successes means the allowance decays with the success rate; a per-request count would have tripled load at exactly this moment.

  5. Step 9 is the honest outcome. The dependency was genuinely degraded and 30% of requests still failed. Retries cannot fix a broken dependency — the goal is to avoid making it worse, and the difference between 30% and 92% is entirely retry policy.

10. When TO Use This

  • Always retry connection-level failures, once. The request provably never arrived, so it is unconditionally safe and it absorbs pool and idle-timeout races (Item 148).

  • Retry idempotent operations under a budget. GET, PUT, DELETE and anything carrying an idempotency key qualify; the budget is what keeps it safe at fleet scale.

  • Honour Retry-After when present. It is the server telling you both that it did not process the request and when it can accept one — ignoring it is how a rate limit becomes a storm.

  • Retry at exactly one layer. Usually the outermost that can judge safety; disable retries in the mesh or gateway if the client does them, and vice versa.

  • Budget in successes, not attempts. ~10% of successful requests, measured over a window, with client-side throttling as the enforcement.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not retry on a timeout without idempotency. You cannot know whether the work completed, and the failure mode is a duplicated side effect — a double charge, a double send, a double write.

  • Do not retry 4xx. The request is wrong; repeating it consumes capacity and is guaranteed to fail identically. Generic "retry on any error" wrappers do this constantly.

  • Do not retry at every hop. kⁿ amplification is the mechanism behind most retry storms, and it is entirely avoidable by choosing one layer.

  • Do not use a fixed attempt count as your only control. It multiplies load exactly when the dependency is failing, which is the opposite of what you need.

  • Scale limit worth naming: retry damage scales with fleet size. A policy that is harmless from one client is a storm from ten thousand, because the dependency sees the sum and no individual client sees anything unusual.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Exponential backoff makes retries safe."

✅ Reality: Backoff spreads retries in time; it does not reduce their number or make an unsafe operation safe. A non-idempotent POST retried with perfect backoff still duplicates the effect, and a fleet retrying with backoff but no budget still multiplies load — just more slowly.

❌ Misconception: "More retries means higher availability."

✅ Reality: Up to a point, then sharply the reverse. Under a partial degradation, retries add load in proportion to the failure rate, which raises the failure rate. Past a threshold, more retries strictly reduce goodput — which is why budgets exist and why the count is not the knob.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Retrying a 500 is fine because the request obviously failed."

✅ Reality: A 500 means the server encountered an error, not that nothing happened. It may have written a row, sent a message and then failed on the response — so a retry can duplicate a partially-applied effect. Only idempotency, or an idempotency key, makes it safe, and the status code alone never does.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Leading with backoff and jitter. They are the well-known part and the least important one. Gating comes first — may this be retried at all? — then the budget, and only then how the attempts are spaced.

Not knowing that a timeout is ambiguous. It is the single most important distinction in this note: connection-level failures are always safe, timeouts never are without idempotency. Collapsing them is how duplicate charges happen.

Ignoring amplification along the chain. kⁿ is checkable arithmetic and forecloses the "each hop retrying is more resilient" intuition immediately.

Treating the attempt count as the control. A count multiplies load under degradation; a budget denominated in successes decays. Naming that inversion unprompted is the strongest signal available on this topic.

Stopping at the client. The storm's damage is at the server, and the server's own protections — load shedding, circuit breaking — are what stop it when client policy fails (Item 151). An answer that is entirely client-side has covered half the system.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Retry budget, typical ~10% of successful requests Denominated in successes so it decays under failure Amazon Builders' Library; Google SRE: Handling Overload
Amplification, n hops × k attempts kⁿ 3 hops × 3 attempts = 27 Direct calculation
Expected multiplier at failure rate p 1 + p + p² + … p = 0.4, k = 3 → 1.56×; p = 0.9 → 2.71× Geometric series
Connection-level retries Unconditionally safe The request never reached the application Derived; RFC 9110 §9.2.2 for the idempotency contract

Methods idempotent by definition GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE POST is not — it needs a key RFC 9110 §9.2.2

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency A retry adds at least one timeout plus backoff to the failed request's latency — paid by the slowest requests
💰 Cost Retried model calls cost real money twice; retried compute costs capacity at the worst moment
🔒 Security / visibility An unbudgeted retry policy is a self-inflicted denial of service against your own dependency
📈 Scale Damage scales with fleet size and with failure rate simultaneously — the two multiply
🔧 Ops complexity Gating rules per operation, a budget per dependency, and exactly one retrying layer to agree on
🐛 Debuggability Retries hide transient failures, so the first symptom of a degrading dependency is often latency, not errors

16. Real World Usage

Client-side throttling from the Google SRE book is the canonical budget implementation. Clients track their own success and rejection counts and probabilistically drop requests when the ratio degrades, which means the fleet self-limits without any coordination — the property that makes it work at scale where a central rate limiter would itself become a dependency.

Idempotency keys are how payment APIs make retries legal. The client generates a key per logical operation, the server records it, and a repeat returns the original result instead of acting again. That single mechanism converts the most dangerous retry in this note into a safe one, which is why it is standard across payment providers (Item 155).

Retry storms are one of the most common shapes in public postmortems. The recurring pattern is identical: a trigger causes partial failure, unbudgeted client retries multiply load, the service saturates, and recovery attempts fail because accumulated retries arrive at once. The lesson consistently drawn is that the fix belongs in the client library's defaults rather than in each service's configuration.

📚 Reference Links

  • The state machine, named and specified — martinfowler.com: Circuit Breaker

  • Shedding to protect goodput under overload — Amazon Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload

  • Why a saturated server must reject rather than queue — Google SRE Book: Handling Overload

  • Concurrency limits as the proxy-side implementation — Envoy: Circuit breaking

  • Bonus — Amazon Builders' Library: Fairness in multi-tenant systems

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three breaker states? Closed (passing), open (failing fast), half-open (one trial request).
Which side does each pattern protect? Breaker protects the caller; shedding protects the callee; bulkheads protect peers.
What does Envoy call a circuit breaker? Concurrency limits — max connections, pending requests, active requests. No timed states.
Why shed rather than queue? Queueing past capacity converts latency into timeouts and produces zero goodput.
What must a breaker have to be safe? A fallback. Failing fast without one just moves the error closer to the user.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three patterns, three different beneficiaries. A circuit breaker protects the caller: after enough failures it stops calling a broken dependency and fails fast, freeing threads that would otherwise block. A bulkhead protects peers: separate connection pools or thread pools per dependency so one slow dependency cannot consume the resources every other call needs. Load shedding protects the callee: a saturated server rejects excess work immediately rather than queueing it, because queueing past capacity produces timeouts instead of responses. The unifying idea is that failing fast preserves capacity, and queueing indefinitely destroys it.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through the breaker states, and say what "circuit breaker" means in Envoy.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the term names two different mechanisms.

The classical breaker is a state machine keyed on failure rate. Closed is normal operation, with failures counted over a window. When failures cross a threshold it trips open: every call fails immediately without touching the dependency, which frees the caller's threads and removes load from the callee. After a cooldown it moves to half-open and admits a small number of trial requests — success closes it, failure reopens it with a longer cooldown. The half-open state is what makes recovery automatic without a stampede.

Envoy's "circuit breakers" are something else: concurrency limits at the connection pool — maximum connections, pending requests, active requests and retries, per cluster. Reaching a limit causes immediate local rejection with no timed states and no half-open probing. It closes again the instant outstanding work drops below the limit.

The distinction matters because they detect different things. A failure-rate breaker triggers on errors; a concurrency limit triggers on slowness, which is the more common production failure. A dependency that is slow but returning 200s never trips a failure-rate breaker, and saturates a concurrency limit immediately. That is why proxies prefer the concurrency form and why a system with only a failure-rate breaker is blind to brownouts.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

When is a circuit breaker the wrong tool?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up after someone proposes breakers everywhere.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know a breaker only helps if there is something useful to do when it opens.

A breaker converts a slow failure into a fast one. That is valuable only if the caller has something better to do with the time — serve a cached value, return a degraded response, omit an optional section, queue the work for later. If the call is mandatory and has no fallback, opening the breaker just returns the error faster, which is a marginal improvement in latency and no improvement in availability. Worse, it can reduce availability: requests that would have succeeded on a struggling-but-alive dependency are now rejected because the breaker is open.

The second failure is oscillation. A breaker with a short cooldown on a dependency that is at the edge of capacity will open, close on a successful probe, be immediately overwhelmed by the resumed traffic, and open again — a flapping pattern that is worse than either extreme because clients experience random failures with no stable behaviour. Longer cooldowns with backoff, and admitting traffic gradually rather than all at once on close, are the mitigations.

My rule: breakers where a fallback exists, concurrency limits (bulkheads) everywhere as the general protection, and load shedding on the server regardless. A breaker on a mandatory dependency is mostly cosmetic; a bulkhead around it is not, because it stops that dependency's slowness from consuming the threads every other request needs.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

A server is at 100% utilisation and its goodput is near zero. What is happening and what fixes it?

📍 Seen in the wild: the overload postmortem, and the clearest argument for shedding.

It is queueing past capacity, and every queued request is being discarded after the work is done. Once arrival rate exceeds service rate, the queue grows without bound, so queue wait grows without bound, so requests exceed their clients' timeouts while still queued. The server then dequeues them and does the work — for a client that has already given up — and the response goes nowhere. Utilisation reads 100% because the server is genuinely busy, and goodput is near zero because none of that work reaches anyone.

It presents as the distinctive combination of full utilisation, near-zero successful responses, and a latency distribution whose p50 exceeds the client timeout. Restarting produces a brief recovery followed by immediate re-collapse as the queued and retried backlog arrives at once (Item 150).

The fix is to reject early rather than queue. Bound the queue explicitly and return 503 immediately when it is full, so rejection costs microseconds instead of a full service time. Better, use latency-based admission: if the current queue wait already exceeds the request's remaining deadline, drop it before doing any work — this is where deadline propagation pays off, because the server can compute whether the work is still wanted (Item 149). And shed by priority rather than uniformly: reject bulk and retry traffic before interactive requests, so the fraction you do serve is the fraction that matters. The counter-intuitive result worth stating is that a server which rejects 40% of requests instantly has far higher goodput than one which accepts everything and completes almost none.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design overload protection for a multi-tenant inference platform.

🎯 Really testing: whether you combine all three patterns and handle the fairness dimension that multi-tenancy adds.

The dominating constraint is that GPU capacity is fixed and expensive, so the system cannot scale out of an overload on the timescale of the incident — which means admission control is the only real lever, and it has to be fair across tenants or one tenant's burst starves everyone.

Layered: bulkheads first, as per-tenant concurrency limits, so a single tenant cannot occupy the whole fleet regardless of how much it sends. This is the most important control because it makes the failure isolated rather than global. Load shedding second, at the gateway, with priority classes — interactive requests above batch, first attempts above retries — and latency-based admission so a request whose deadline cannot be met is rejected before consuming a GPU second rather than after. Circuit breakers third, on the calls that have fallbacks — a smaller model, a cached response, a degraded answer — and deliberately not on the mandatory path, where they would only convert slow failures into fast ones.

Retries interact with all of this and must be budgeted, or shedding creates the storm it exists to prevent: rejected requests are exactly the ones clients retry (Item 150). Rejections should carry Retry-After so well-behaved clients back off correctly.

The failure I would monitor first is goodput versus utilisation, together on one graph, because their divergence is the definitive overload signature and neither alone shows it. Second is per-tenant admitted share against the limit, which is the fairness measurement and the thing a customer will ask about. Third is shed rate by priority class, because shedding that is hitting interactive traffic while batch still flows means the classification is wrong.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Pattern Protects Triggers on Mechanism When you'd actually pick it
Circuit breaker (state machine) The caller Failure rate over a window Open → half-open → closed The call has a fallback worth serving
Concurrency limit / bulkhead Peers of the call Outstanding work past a limit Immediate local rejection Always — catches slowness, not just errors
Thread/pool isolation Peers of the call Pool exhaustion Separate pools per dependency One dependency must not starve the others
Load shedding The callee Queue depth or predicted deadline miss Reject with 503 + Retry-After Always on any server that can be overloaded
Priority shedding The callee, fairly Same, per class Reject bulk before interactive Mixed workloads or multi-tenant
Rate limiting The callee, per client Request rate per identity Reject past a quota Known clients with agreed quotas

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

Design axis: who is being protected — the caller, its neighbours, or the callee?

📖 Story — the ship

  • Circuit breaker — the engine room stops feeding a seized propeller shaft. The shaft is broken either way; what you save is the engine.

  • Bulkhead — the hull is divided into sealed compartments, so a breach floods one and the ship stays afloat.

  • Load shedding — the lifeboat is full, so the crew turns people away at the rail instead of letting it swamp and drown everyone aboard.

  • Priority shedding — the crew fills that lifeboat in an agreed order rather than first-come, so the places that exist go to the people they were meant for.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Stopping the feed to a seized shaft = opening the breaker to stop calling a failed dependency

  • Sealed compartments = per-dependency pools, so one flood does not reach the rest

  • Turning people away at the rail = rejecting at admission, before the work is done, which is what preserves goodput

  • Filling in an agreed order = priority classes and per-tenant limits

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Goodput, not utilisation, is the quantity being defended. Under overload with unbounded queueing, throughput of useful work collapses toward zero while utilisation sits at 100%, because completed work arrives after its client gave up. Shedding trades a known rejection rate for a preserved completion rate: rejecting a fraction r immediately means the remaining (1 − r) is served inside its deadline, and total goodput is (1 − r) × λ rather than approximately zero. The counter-intuitive consequence is that rejecting more can serve more, and it is the single most useful thing to be able to say about overload.

Rejection must be far cheaper than service or shedding does not work. If rejecting costs a meaningful fraction of a service time, a saturated server spends its capacity rejecting and the protection fails. This is why admission control belongs as early as possible — at the gateway, before auth, deserialisation or any allocation — and why a 503 from deep inside the application is much weaker than one from the edge.

Latency-based admission is the sharpest form. If the current queue wait already exceeds the request's remaining deadline, the work is provably wasted, so dropping it costs nothing and saves a full service time. This requires knowing the deadline, which is the practical payoff of deadline propagation (Item 149).

Bulkheads bound the blast radius arithmetically. With one shared pool of N workers and a dependency whose service time rises to W, Little's Law says the dependency occupies λ × W workers — and when that exceeds N, every other call starves. Partitioning into per-dependency pools of Nᵢ caps that at Nᵢ, so the failure is contained by construction rather than by hoping the numbers work out.

7. Why It Matters in Production

These three patterns are what separate "one dependency degraded" from "the whole service is down". The mechanism is always the same: a slow dependency occupies resources, resources run out, and every unrelated request fails too. Bulkheads bound it, breakers release it, shedding stops the queue from forming in the first place.

The observable that matters is goodput plotted against utilisation on one graph. Their divergence — utilisation climbing while goodput falls — is the definitive overload signature, and neither metric alone shows it. Most dashboards carry utilisation and request rate, both of which look healthy during exactly this failure.

The second is rejection rate by reason: breaker-open, concurrency-limit, queue-full, priority-shed. Those four are different problems with different fixes, and collapsing them into one "5xx" bucket hides which control is actually firing.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Envoy: bulkheads (concurrency limits) plus outlier ejection. Note there are no timed states.
circuit_breakers:
  thresholds:
    - priority: DEFAULT
      max_connections: 100        # bulkhead: this cluster can never take more
      max_pending_requests: 50    # queue bound - past this, immediate local 503
      max_requests: 200           # concurrent in-flight cap
      max_retries: 10             # retries are capped SEPARATELY - storm protection
outlier_detection:
  consecutive_5xx: 5              # eject a bad host (Section 11, Item 113)
  max_ejection_percent: 50        # never eject more than half - fail open

# Server side: latency-based admission. Reject BEFORE the work, not after.
def admit(request, queue):
    projected_wait = queue.depth * queue.mean_service_time
    if projected_wait > request.remaining_deadline:
        return reject(503, retry_after=jittered(1, 5))   # provably wasted work
    if queue.depth > HARD_LIMIT and request.priority == BULK:
        return reject(503, retry_after=jittered(5, 30))  # shed bulk before interactive
    return queue.enqueue(request)

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

A service with 100 workers and 40ms service time — capacity ~2,500 rps — receiving 4,000 rps.

🎬 UNPROTECTED: unbounded queue
📥 [1] λ=4000 rps, μ=2500 rps → queue grows at 1500 req/s
    ▼
⏱️ [2] t=10s: queue = 15,000 → wait = 15000/2500 = 6.0s
    │   client timeout is 2s → every request now times out WHILE QUEUED
    ▼
💥 [3] server dequeues and serves them anyway — for clients that left
    │   utilisation 100%  |  goodput ≈ 0 rps  |  p50 latency 6s > 2s timeout
    ▼
🔁 [4] clients retry (no budget) → λ rises to 6000 → queue grows faster

🎬 PROTECTED: bounded queue + latency-based admission
📥 [5] λ=4000 rps, capacity 2500 rps
    ▼
🛡️ [6] admission: projected_wait = depth x 40ms; reject when > remaining deadline
    │   steady state: queue held at ~50, wait ~20ms
    ▼
✅ [7] admitted 2,500 rps served in ~60ms  |  rejected 1,500 rps in ~0.1ms
    │   goodput 2,500 rps  ← vs ~0 unprotected. Rejecting MORE served MORE.
    ▼
🛡️ [8] priority: bulk sheds first → interactive rejection rate ~5%, bulk ~85%
    ▼
🛡️ [9] per-tenant bulkhead: tenant A's burst capped at its share
    │   tenants B–Z unaffected — failure isolated, not global
    ▼
📉 [10] rejections carry Retry-After with jitter → retries spread, no second wave

  1. Step 3 is the whole argument. 100% utilisation and zero goodput simultaneously. Every capacity metric on the dashboard says the service is working hard, and none says it is achieving nothing.

  2. Step 7 is the counter-intuitive result to state out loud. The protected server rejects 1,500 rps and serves 2,500; the unprotected one rejects nothing and serves approximately none. Rejecting more served more.

  3. Rejection cost is what makes it work — 0.1ms versus 40ms, a 400× difference. If rejection cost a meaningful fraction of service time, the server would saturate on rejections and the protection would fail.

  4. Step 9 is what multi-tenancy adds. Without per-tenant bulkheads, tenant A's burst consumes the shared admission budget and every other tenant sees rejections caused by traffic they did not send.

  5. Step 10 closes the loop with Item 150. Rejected requests are exactly the ones clients retry, so shedding without Retry-After and a client-side budget creates the storm it was meant to prevent.

10. When TO Use This

  • Load shedding on every server that can be overloaded. It is the only control that preserves goodput once demand exceeds capacity, and it must reject at admission rather than after the work.

  • Bulkheads — per-dependency concurrency limits — as the default protection. They catch slowness rather than just errors, which is the more common failure, and they bound blast radius arithmetically.

  • Circuit breakers where a fallback exists. Cached values, degraded responses, omitted optional sections; without one, opening the breaker only returns the error faster.

  • Priority classes wherever workloads are mixed. Shedding bulk and retry traffic before interactive requests means the served fraction is the fraction that matters.

  • Per-tenant limits in any multi-tenant system. Otherwise one tenant's burst is indistinguishable from a platform outage for everyone else.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not add a circuit breaker to a mandatory call with no fallback. It converts a slow error into a fast one and can reject requests that would have succeeded — cosmetic at best, harmful at worst.

  • Do not shed after doing the work. Rejection must cost orders of magnitude less than service, which means admission control at the edge, before auth, parsing or allocation.

  • Do not use a short, fixed breaker cooldown. A dependency at the edge of capacity will oscillate — open, probe, get overwhelmed, reopen — and clients see random failures with no stable behaviour.

  • Do not shed uniformly in a mixed workload. Rejecting interactive requests at the same rate as batch wastes the capacity you did preserve on work nobody is waiting for.

  • Scale limit worth naming: these controls bound damage, they do not create capacity. A system persistently shedding 40% needs more capacity or less demand; shedding is what keeps it serving while you arrange one of those.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures."

✅ Reality: They help the caller stop wasting resources on a dead dependency. They do nothing for the overloaded callee, and nothing for the queue that has already formed. Load shedding at the server is what protects the failing component; the breaker protects everyone calling it.

❌ Misconception: "Rejecting requests hurts availability, so accept everything and do your best."

✅ Reality: Past capacity, accepting everything produces near-zero goodput because completed work arrives after clients have timed out. A server rejecting 40% instantly delivers vastly more successful responses than one accepting 100% and completing almost none.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "A circuit breaker will catch a degraded dependency."

✅ Reality: Only if it is returning errors. A dependency that is slow but returning 200s never trips a failure-rate breaker — and slowness is the more common degradation. Concurrency limits catch it immediately, which is why proxies implement "circuit breaking" as a limit rather than as a state machine.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Using "circuit breaker" without saying which mechanism. The failure-rate state machine and the concurrency limit are both called that, they detect different failures, and a system with only the first is blind to brownouts. Naming both distinguishes reading from operating.

Proposing a breaker with no fallback. The first follow-up is what you serve when it opens, and "an error, but faster" is not an answer. Breakers are only worth it where degradation is possible.

Missing the goodput argument. "Reject more, serve more" is counter-intuitive, checkable and the most persuasive single point available on overload. An answer about shedding that never mentions goodput has described a mechanism without its justification.

Forgetting that rejection must be cheap. Shedding from deep in the application, after auth and deserialisation, consumes the capacity it was meant to preserve.

Stopping before the retry interaction. Rejected requests are precisely the ones clients retry, so shedding without Retry-After and a client budget manufactures a storm (Item 150). The two controls only work as a pair.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Breaker states 3 — closed, open, half-open The half-open probe is what makes recovery automatic martinfowler.com: Circuit Breaker
Envoy circuit breakers Concurrency limits, no timed states Triggers on slowness, not just errors Envoy: Circuit breaking
Goodput under unbounded queueing → 0 at 100% utilisation Work completes after clients time out Google SRE: Handling Overload
Rejection cost vs service cost Must be orders of magnitude cheaper ~0.1 ms vs ~40 ms in the trace above Amazon Builders' Library: Load shedding
Bulkhead bound λ × W workers occupied, capped at Nᵢ Little's Law applied to blast radius Derived; Item 152
Retry cap, separate from request cap Envoy max_retries Retries bounded independently of requests Envoy: Circuit breaking

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency All three trade some rejected requests for a bounded, predictable latency on the rest
💰 Cost Shedding avoids paying for work that will be discarded — the cheapest capacity you will ever recover
🔒 Security / visibility Admission control doubles as abuse protection; per-tenant limits are also a fairness control
📈 Scale These bound damage; they do not add capacity. Persistent shedding is a capacity signal, not a solution
🔧 Ops complexity Thresholds, cooldowns, priority classes and per-tenant limits are a lot of tuning surface, and all of it drifts
🐛 Debuggability Rejections must be distinguishable by reason, or four different controls all look like one 503

16. Real World Usage

Envoy shipping concurrency limits rather than a failure-rate state machine is the strongest available signal about which mechanism matters in practice. The reference proxy chose the form that catches slowness, because brownouts are more common than hard failures and a state machine misses them entirely.

Priority-based shedding is standard in large multi-tenant systems because uniform rejection wastes preserved capacity on work nobody is waiting for. The Builders' Library's fairness treatment makes the same point from the tenant angle: without per-tenant limits, one customer's burst is indistinguishable from an outage for every other customer.

The goodput-versus-utilisation divergence is the canonical overload signature in the SRE literature, and its practical value is that it is visible on one graph while every other metric on a standard dashboard — utilisation, request rate, CPU — reads as healthy or even good during the failure.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym. Goodput is worth defining as distinct from throughput: throughput counts work completed, goodput counts work completed and delivered to a client still waiting for it. The gap between them is the entire subject of this note.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 149-timeout-hierarchy.md — fast failure requires bounded calls in the first place

  • 150-retries-done-right.md — the client-side half; rejections are what clients retry

  • Section 11 113-outlier-detection-circuit-breaking.md — the proxy-level implementation

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 152-queueing-theory.md — why goodput collapses past ~70–80% utilisation

  • 156-graceful-degradation-backpressure.md — the fallbacks that make breakers worth having

  • 157-cascading-failures.md — the failure these three patterns exist to stop

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Autoscaling — add capacity instead of shedding; too slow for the timescale of an overload

  • Rate limiting per client — bounds demand by identity rather than by system state (Section 7, Item 69)

  • Queue-based decoupling — absorb bursts asynchronously where the work permits it

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Retry budgets — without them, shedding creates the storm it prevents (Item 150)

  • Deadline propagation — enables latency-based admission (Item 149)

  • Health checks and outlier ejection — removing bad hosts before these controls are needed (Section 11, Item 112)

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Usually as "what happens when your dependency gets slow?" — and the weak answer is "we have retries and timeouts". The strong answer separates the three beneficiaries, puts a bulkhead around the dependency unconditionally, adds a breaker only where a fallback exists, and puts shedding on the server. The follow-up is almost always the goodput argument, and being able to state "rejecting more serves more" with the arithmetic behind it is what carries it.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× Shared worker pool starves when one dependency slows Per-dependency bulkheads; bound each pool explicitly
100× Admission decisions themselves cost capacity; tuning drifts across services Shed at the edge before parsing; centralise policy in the gateway or mesh
1000× Per-tenant fairness becomes the dominant concern; global limits are meaningless Per-tenant quotas with priority classes; fairness measured and reported per tenant

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: an unbounded queue somewhere in the path — a framework default nobody set — that makes every other control irrelevant.

  • 100×: breaker oscillation on dependencies sitting at the edge of capacity, producing random client-visible failures.

  • Operational: shedding without Retry-After and without client budgets, so rejected traffic returns immediately as a retry storm.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Goodput and utilisation on one graph. Their divergence is the overload signature; neither alone shows it.

  • Rejections by reason — breaker-open, concurrency-limit, queue-full, priority-shed. Four different problems, four different fixes.

  • Per-tenant admitted share against limit. The fairness measurement, and the number a customer will ask about by name.

  • Breaker state transitions per minute. A high rate is oscillation, which is worse for clients than a breaker that stays open.

📚 Reference Links

  • Why a saturated server must reject rather than queue — Google SRE Book: Handling Overload

  • Queue growth as the mechanism behind cascading failure — Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

  • Bounded queues and load shedding in practice — Amazon Builders' Library: Using load shedding to avoid overload

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Little's Law? L = λW. Items in system = arrival rate × time in system. Holds for any stable system.
The utilisation formula for wait time? Wait ∝ ρ / (1 − ρ). At ρ=0.5 the factor is 1; at 0.9 it is 9; at 0.99 it is 99.
Why does p99 explode before p50? The queueing term is a distribution; its tail grows far faster than its mean.
What does variability do? Multiplies the wait. Same utilisation, higher variance in service time = longer queues.
Practical utilisation ceiling? ~70–80% for latency-sensitive work — beyond it, each increment costs disproportionate latency.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Two results carry almost all the practical weight. Little's Law, L = λW, says the number of items in a system equals arrival rate times time in system — it holds for any stable system regardless of distribution, and it is how you size pools, thread counts and connection limits. The utilisation curve says waiting time scales as ρ/(1−ρ), so it is roughly flat until about 70% and then rises hyperbolically: at 90% utilisation the queueing factor is nine, at 99% it is ninety-nine. That non-linearity is why p99 collapses while average utilisation still looks comfortable.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why does latency explode near full utilisation rather than degrading smoothly?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can explain the shape of the curve rather than quote a threshold.

Because a queue only drains during idle moments, and idle moments are what utilisation removes. At 50% utilisation the server is idle half the time, so any backlog clears almost immediately. At 90% it is idle a tenth of the time, so a burst takes ten times as long to work off. At 99% there is essentially no slack, and a burst persists almost indefinitely — the queue has no opportunity to shrink.

The standard result for a simple queue is that mean wait scales with ρ/(1−ρ) where ρ is utilisation. The denominator is what produces the explosion: as ρ → 1, the factor grows without bound. That is why "we're only at 85% CPU" is not the reassurance it sounds like — 85% puts the factor at about 5.7, against 1.0 at 50%.

The second driver is variability, and it is the one people omit. Wait time scales with the variance of both arrival and service times, not just their means. A service where every request takes exactly 40ms queues far less at the same utilisation than one where requests take 5ms or 2 seconds — which is precisely the inference workload from Section 13, and the reason request-cost variance and queueing are the same conversation.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

What utilisation should you actually target?

🎯 Really testing: whether you connect the target to the workload's variance and its latency requirement, rather than quoting 70%.

It depends on two things: how latency-sensitive the work is, and how variable it is. For latency-sensitive, high-variance work — user-facing requests, especially inference — the practical ceiling is around 60–70%, because the queueing factor is already 1.5–2.3 there and variance multiplies it further. Pushing to 85% roughly triples the queueing term for a workload that already has a heavy tail.

For throughput-oriented, uniform work — batch processing, asynchronous jobs, queue consumers — you can and should run much hotter, 85–95%, because nobody is waiting on an individual item and the variance is low. Idle capacity there is pure waste.

The subtlety worth raising is that utilisation is measured per server but latency is experienced per request, and a fleet averaging 70% may contain servers at 95% if load balancing is uneven — which is where this note meets Section 11's algorithms. A fleet's average utilisation is a poor proxy for its queueing behaviour when max-to-median is 3. So the honest target is a utilisation ceiling plus a distribution requirement, and the second one is what most capacity plans omit.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Utilisation ρ Queueing factor ρ/(1−ρ) Practical meaning Suitable for
0.50 1.0 Wait ≈ one service time Comfortable for anything
0.70 2.3 Wait ≈ 2× service time The usual ceiling for user-facing work
0.80 4.0 Wait ≈ 4× service time Uniform, latency-tolerant work
0.90 9.0 Wait ≈ 9× service time Batch only
0.95 19.0 Wait ≈ 19× service time Async queue consumers
0.99 99.0 Effectively unbounded Nothing with a deadline

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Little's Law: L = λW. Mean items in the system equals mean arrival rate times mean time in system. It is distribution-free and holds for any stable system, which is what makes it the workhorse: pool sizing (Item 148), thread counts, concurrency limits (Item 151) and in-flight request caps all fall straight out of it. At 500 rps and 40ms, L = 20. At 50 rps and 20 seconds — a model call — L = 1,000.

The utilisation curve: wait ∝ ρ/(1−ρ). For an M/M/1 queue, mean queue wait is W_q = ρ/(μ(1−ρ)) — one service time multiplied by the queueing factor. The table above is that factor evaluated. The key property is the pole at ρ = 1: capacity planning is not linear, and the last 10% of utilisation costs more latency than the first 70%.

Variability multiplies it. The Kingman approximation gives W_q ≈ (ρ/(1−ρ)) × ((c_a² + c_s²)/2) × service_time, where c_a and c_s are the coefficients of variation of arrivals and service. Two consequences: a workload with highly variable service times queues far worse at the same utilisation, and reducing variance is a latency fix that does not require more capacity — which is what batching, request shaping and separating fast from slow endpoints actually achieve.

Percentiles are worse than means. Every formula above is for the mean wait. The tail of the waiting-time distribution grows faster still, which is why p99 degrades visibly while p50 and average utilisation still look healthy. That gap is the reason capacity decisions made on averages consistently under-provision (Item 153).

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not target high utilisation for latency-sensitive work. Past ~70% each additional increment costs disproportionate latency, and the cost is concentrated in the tail users actually notice.

  • Do not size from means when service time is variable. Little's Law gives the mean; a pool or thread count sized to it is short exactly when a batch of slow requests arrives.

  • Do not read fleet-average utilisation as the queueing input. Uneven load balancing means individual servers can sit far above the average, and queueing is per server (Section 11, Item 109).

  • Do not treat these formulas as predictions. They are single-queue idealisations; their value is the shape — the pole at full utilisation, and variance as a multiplier — not the specific number.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "We have headroom — we're only at 85% utilisation."

✅ Reality: The queueing factor at 85% is about 5.7 against 1.0 at 50%, so requests are already waiting several service times. Utilisation is not a linear measure of headroom, and the region where it looks comfortable on a dashboard is where latency is already degrading.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Reducing latency requires more capacity."

✅ Reality: Reducing variance also works, and often costs nothing. Kingman's formula has variance as a direct multiplier, so separating slow endpoints from fast ones, capping request sizes, or shaping traffic reduces queueing at unchanged utilisation — which is why splitting a mixed workload into two pools frequently improves both.
